bull.argument: The filing shows a business with strong, accelerating momentum. Consolidated net sales rose 12% to $716.9 billion in 2025, and AWS grew 20% to $128.7 billion, with the segment's operating income climbing to $45.6 billion. Operating income reached $80.0 billion, up from $68.6 billion, and operating cash flow rose to $139.5 billion from $115.9 billion. Management is deliberately reinvesting: cash capital expenditures reached $128.3 billion, mostly for technology infrastructure that supports AWS growth, and the company expects these to increase in 2026. Management also states that the 2025 Tax Act significantly decreased cash taxes and is expected to have a similar effect in 2026, which supports cash generation. Liquidity is substantial, with cash and marketable securities at $123.0 billion and no borrowings under its revolving facilities or commercial paper as of year-end. The risks are real, including ongoing antitrust investigations and the FTC settlement, and free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion from $38.2 billion. Still, that decline is the result of the AWS build-out the filing describes, not a weakening of the core business.

claims.claim: Consolidated net sales grew 12% in 2025, and AWS sales grew 20%.
claims.quote: AWS sales increased 20% in 2025, compared to the prior year. The sales growth primarily reflects increased customer usage

claims.claim: Operating cash flow rose substantially, supporting the business's cash generation.
Cash capital expenditures are directed toward infrastructure supporting AWS growth, and are expected to rise in 2026.
claims.quote: which primarily reflect investments in technology infrastructure (the majority of which is to support AWS business growth) and in additional capacity to support our fulfillment network, both of which we expect to increase in 2026

bear.argument: The opponent's growth story rests on operating income and operating cash flow, but the filing shows the cash that reaches shareholders collapsed. Free cash flow fell from $38.2 billion to $11.2 billion because cash capital expenditures rose to $128.3 billion, and management says these will increase again in 2026. Investing outflows reached $142.5 billion, and the company now relies on new financing, with long-term debt rising from $52.6 billion to $65.6 billion and financing inflows of $25.0 billion in 2025. Earnings quality is also weaker than headline operating income suggests. Net income was lifted by a $15.2 billion other income gain, primarily an upward adjustment on the Anthropic preferred stock, a non-operating and valuation-driven item. Operating income absorbed a $2.5 billion FTC settlement and $2.7 billion of severance costs. Management also warns that the company may not recoup its significant investments in new technologies, and that open investigations, including into AWS, could materially affect results. Shareholders are being asked to fund a very large, expanding capital program with uncertain returns.

claims.claim: Free cash flow collapsed as capital spending surged, leaving far less cash for shareholders.
Management expects capital spending to rise again, so cash pressure may persist.
claims.quote: which primarily reflect investments in technology infrastructure (the majority of which is to support AWS business growth) and in additional capacity to support our fulfillment network, both of which we expect to increase in 2026

claims.claim: Reported earnings were boosted by a non-operating valuation gain rather than core operations.
claims.quote: The net gain of $15.2 billion in 2025 is primarily from an upward adjustment for observable changes in price relating to our nonvoting

bull.argument: The bear case is right that free cash flow fell to $11.2 billion from $38.2 billion, but the filing ties that drop to a deliberate build-out rather than a broken core. Capex of $128.3 billion is mostly technology infrastructure supporting AWS, and AWS operating income still rose to $45.6 billion on 20% sales growth. Operating cash flow itself climbed to $139.5 billion, so the business generated more cash before investment; the squeeze comes from spending. The $15.2 billion other income gain is non-operating, and we should set it aside. Strip it out and the operating story stands on its own: consolidated operating income rose to $80.0 billion even after absorbing the $2.5 billion FTC charge and $2.7 billion of severance. On financing, debt rose to $65.6 billion, but cash and marketable securities were $123.0 billion and there were no borrowings under the revolving facilities or commercial paper at year-end, so liquidity is not strained. The filing does warn that new-technology investments may not be recouped and that AWS investigations could matter. Those are real risks, and the filing presents them as possibilities, not as results already in hand.

claims.claim: Operating cash flow grew while capital spending rose, showing the cash squeeze comes from investment, not weaker operations.
AWS sales growth continued at 20%, with the growth driven by customer usage.
claims.quote: AWS sales increased 20% in 2025, compared to the prior year. The sales growth primarily reflects increased customer usage

claims.claim: Year-end liquidity was strong, with no borrowings outstanding under the revolving credit facilities or commercial paper programs.
claims.quote: We had no borrowings outstanding under the two unsecured revolving credit facilities or the commercial paper programs as of December 31, 2025.

bear.argument: The opponent concedes the core issue: cash returned from the business fell sharply. Free cash flow dropped from $38.2 billion to $11.2 billion, and the filing says cash capital expenditures of $128.3 billion will rise again in 2026. Calling this a deliberate build-out does not change what shareholders receive. Operating cash flow growth is real, but nearly all of it is consumed by capex, and the filing states that spending will increase, so the squeeze is likely to continue. The opponent also says liquidity is not strained, yet the filing shows long-term debt up from $52.6 billion to $65.6 billion and $25.0 billion of debt inflows in 2025. Cash of $123.0 billion is largely offset by these obligations and by $87.3 billion of long-term lease liabilities. Setting aside the $15.2 billion gain does not remove the earnings problem: that gain was the main driver of higher pre-tax results, while operating income absorbed $2.5 billion for the FTC settlement and $2.7 billion of severance. The risks are not merely hypothetical. The filing says the company may fail to recoup significant investments, and that AWS investigations could materially affect results. A business whose free cash flow fell 71% is a risky place to park capital.

claims.claim: Free cash flow fell sharply as capital spending rose, reducing cash available to shareholders.
Management expects capital spending to increase again in 2026.
claims.quote: both of which we expect to increase in 2026

claims.claim: The company is relying more on debt, with long-term debt rising in 2025.
claims.quote: Our long-term debt was $52.6 billion and $65.6 billion as of December 31, 2024 and 2025.

judge.reasoning: All quotes are verified on both sides, so the comparison turns on argument quality. The bear side used more decisive evidence (FCF collapse from $38.2B to $11.2B, rising long-term debt, and the non-operating $15.2B gain) and directly rebutted the bull's reliance on operating cash flow by noting capex absorbs nearly all of it. The bull answered well by conceding the FCF drop and setting aside the gain, but it did not fully address the rising debt and lease obligations, so the bear edges out the win.
